Q221967.title: Brusilov Offensive
Q221967.place: Eastern Front: Volhynia, eastern Galicia and Bukovina (today north-western Ukraine)
paras: The Brusilov Offensive was the great Russian attack on the Eastern Front of the First World War that began on 4 June 1916 and lasted into the autumn (HISTORY says it was shut down on 20 September; Wikipedia says late September). It was led by General Aleksei Brusilov, commander of Russia's South-Western Front, against the armies of Austria-Hungary and, increasingly, Germany, in the region that is now north-western Ukraine. Wikipedia calls it the Russian Empire's greatest feat of arms in the war.

Under the Chantilly agreement of December 1915 the Allies had promised simultaneous offensives in 1916. The Germans were attacking at Verdun, and in May the Austro-Hungarians struck the Italians in South Tyrol (the Trentino), so Italy pressed urgently for a relief offensive in the east. Brusilov insisted on attacking along a broad front rather than at a single point; according to Manfried Rauchensteiner's history of Austria-Hungary in the war, the Russian chief of staff Mikhail Alekseev begged him on the evening of 3 June to postpone and narrow the attack, and Brusilov refused.

The offensive opened with a carefully prepared barrage that tore gaps in the Austro-Hungarian wire and buried defenders in their dugouts, and the infantry then stormed the first lines from close range. Kaledin's 8th Army broke the Austro-Hungarian 4th Army of Archduke Joseph Ferdinand around Lutsk, which the Russians occupied within days; Wikipedia says the 4th Army fell from 117,800 men to 35,000 in four days. Further south the Austro-Hungarian 7th Army was also driven back, and Russian forces went on to take cities including Brody, Kolomyia and Chernivtsi and reach the Carpathian foothills. Austria-Hungary had to halt its Italian offensive, and Germany sent divisions from the west to shore up its ally.

The cost was enormous on both sides, and the figures differ widely. Wikipedia gives 500,000 to 1,000,000 Russian casualties, about 616,000 Austro-Hungarian and 148,000 to 350,000 German, while HISTORY puts Austro-Hungarian losses at 1.5 million, including 400,000 prisoners. The offensive eased pressure on the French at Verdun and on the Italians, inflicted losses on the Austro-Hungarian army from which it never recovered, and brought Romania into the war on the Allied side. But Russia's own losses were so heavy that, as Wikipedia notes, many historians see them as contributing to the collapse of the Russian army and the revolution of 1917.

Q187152.title: Balfour Declaration
Q187152.place: London (issued by the British government); concerning Palestine, then Ottoman
paras: The Balfour Declaration was a short statement of British policy issued during the First World War. It took the form of a letter dated 2 November 1917 from the foreign secretary, Arthur James Balfour, to Lord Rothschild, conveying on behalf of the government a 'declaration of sympathy with Jewish Zionist aspirations' that the Cabinet had approved, and asking him to pass it to the Zionist Federation. Its single sentence said that the government viewed 'with favour the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people' and would use its best endeavours to bring this about, 'it being clearly understood' that nothing would be done to prejudice 'the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities in Palestine', or the rights and political status of Jews in any other country. The text appeared in the press on 9 November. Palestine was then an Ottoman region; Wikipedia describes its population as an overwhelming Arab majority, mostly Muslim with Christians, and a small Jewish minority.

Britain had been at war with the Ottoman Empire since November 1914. In early 1915 Herbert Samuel, a Jewish member of the Cabinet, circulated a memorandum proposing British support for Zionist aims in Palestine. After David Lloyd George replaced H. H. Asquith as prime minister in December 1916, formal negotiations with the Zionist leadership began: Sir Mark Sykes met them on 7 February 1917, the French diplomat Jules Cambon sent the Zionist envoy Nahum Sokolow a letter of sympathy dated 4 June, and on 19 June Balfour asked Rothschild and Chaim Weizmann to submit a draft.

Drafts were discussed in the War Cabinet in September and October, with submissions from Zionist and non-Zionist Jews but, as Wikipedia notes, no representation of Palestine's Arab population. The leading Jewish opponent was Edwin Montagu, secretary of state for India; the two safeguard clauses were added in early October to meet such objections. President Woodrow Wilson agreed to the release on 6 October (Wikipedia), and the War Cabinet authorised it on 31 October. According to Wikipedia, the ministers expected propaganda benefits among Jews, especially in Russia and America; the Encyclopaedia Judaica also stresses the wish to forestall German approaches to the Zionists and Lloyd George's aim of bringing Palestine under British control.

Reactions differed sharply. Wikipedia describes the declaration as the first public support for Zionism by a major power, which gave the movement new momentum; the Encyclopaedia Judaica records an enthusiastic response among Jewish communities, above all in Russia, and Jews in Palestine kept 2 November as Balfour Day from 1918 until the Second World War. According to Wikipedia, the Muslim and Christian Arabs who made up almost 90% of Palestine's population strongly opposed it; on 3 November 1918 the Muslim-Christian Association handed the military governor, Ronald Storrs, a protest petition signed by more than 100 notables. The Sharif of Mecca and other Arab leaders regarded it as a breach of earlier British promises made in the McMahon–Hussein correspondence. The British government rejected that reading: its White Paper of June 1922 stated that Sir Henry McMahon's letter of 24 October 1915 had excluded Palestine west of the Jordan from the pledge of Arab independence. Among the Allies, the Encyclopaedia Judaica says that Russia, France, Italy and the United States had approved the declaration in advance; Wikipedia dates the first endorsement by a foreign government to 27 December 1917 (Serbia's government in exile), with French and Italian endorsements following in 1918.

British forces took Jerusalem on 9 December 1917. At San Remo on 25 April 1920 the Allied powers assigned Palestine to Britain as a League of Nations mandate, making Britain responsible for putting the declaration into effect. The Mandate for Palestine, dated in London on 24 July 1922, repeated the declaration in its preamble, made Britain responsible for securing the Jewish national home and developing self-governing institutions while safeguarding the civil and religious rights of all inhabitants, and required it to facilitate Jewish immigration without prejudicing the rights and position of the rest of the population; Wikipedia notes that it was formalised in September 1923. In its June 1922 White Paper the British government interpreted the declaration as meaning a national home founded 'in Palestine', not the conversion of Palestine as a whole, with immigration limited by the country's economic capacity. Intercommunal conflict in Mandatory Palestine began in 1920, and in 1939, according to Wikipedia, the British government acknowledged that the wishes and interests of the local population should have been taken into account. Wikipedia regards the declaration as having led indirectly to the emergence of the State of Israel.

Q659745.title: Italian Front
Q659745.place: Border between Italy and Austria-Hungary: the Isonzo, the Karst, the Trentino and the Alps, later the Piave
paras: The Italian front was the theatre of the First World War along the border between the Kingdom of Italy and Austria-Hungary, fought from 1915 to 1918. Although Italy had been allied with Germany and Austria-Hungary, it stayed neutral when the war began in August 1914; relations in the alliance were already strained by Italian claims to Habsburg lands. In the secret Treaty of London of 26 April 1915, Britain, France and Russia promised Italy territory at Austria-Hungary's expense; Wikipedia lists Trento, Trieste, South Tyrol, Istria and northern Dalmatia. Italy declared war on Austria-Hungary on 23 May 1915.

The front ran for hundreds of kilometres from the Adriatic coast along the Karst plateau and the Isonzo (Soča) river up into the Alps; The Past puts its length at almost 400 miles. In the mountains both sides faced avalanches, extreme cold and difficult supply. The main Italian effort was on the Isonzo, aimed at Gorizia and Trieste: twelve battles were fought there between June 1915 and October 1917, beginning on 23 June 1915. Despite superior numbers and material, the Italians made little headway; in August 1916, when Austria-Hungary had to move troops east to face Russia's Brusilov offensive, they took Gorizia in the Sixth Battle. An Austro-Hungarian offensive from the Trentino in May 1916 made early gains before being pushed back. According to The Past, Austria-Hungary fought alone on this front for more than two years, because Germany refused to intervene against Italy until the autumn of 1917.

After the Eleventh Battle of the Isonzo in 1917 (LeMO: 48 Italian divisions and 6,800 guns on a 70-kilometre front) the Austro-Hungarian line was close to collapse. German troops were then sent to help, and on 24 October 1917 Austro-Hungarian and German forces opened the Twelfth Battle of the Isonzo, known as Caporetto, with gas shells and infiltration tactics. Within two weeks they had broken through to the Piave river. Under a new chief of staff, Armando Diaz, the Italians held a line on the Piave and Monte Grappa, reinforced by British and French divisions, and in June 1918 they threw back a major Austro-Hungarian attack across the Piave.

In late October 1918, as Austria-Hungary was breaking apart, the Italian army attacked across the Piave towards Vittorio Veneto. The Austro-Hungarian front collapsed; Wikipedia says 300,000 soldiers surrendered on 3 November, the day Italian troops entered Trento and Trieste. The armistice signed at Villa Giusti near Padua on 3 November took effect on 4 November 1918. Wikipedia gives over 531,000 Italian military dead in the war and about 400,000 Austro-Hungarian dead on the Italian front. The treaties of 1919 and 1920 gave Italy Trento, Trieste, South Tyrol and Istria, while northern Dalmatia, except Zara, went to Yugoslavia.

Q278960.title: Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty
Q278960.place: Moscow (signed by the USSR, the United Kingdom and the United States)
paras: The Partial Test Ban Treaty (also called the Limited Test Ban Treaty) was signed in Moscow on 5 August 1963 by the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and the United States. It banned nuclear weapon tests in the atmosphere, in outer space and under water, but not underground. The Office of the Historian of the US State Department calls it the first arms control agreement of the Cold War, concluded between President John F. Kennedy and the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev.

Public concern had been growing over radioactive fallout from atmospheric tests, especially after the first hydrogen bombs of 1952–53; Wikipedia cites the US Castle Bravo test of 1954, whose fallout sickened Japanese fishermen. The three powers began negotiating a comprehensive test ban in 1958 and observed a voluntary moratorium on testing, but talks stalled over verification: the United States and Britain wanted on-site inspections to tell underground tests from earthquakes, while the Soviet Union saw these as a cover for espionage. After the U-2 incident of 1960 the prospects faded, and both sides resumed testing in 1961–62.

The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962, together with worries about the spread of nuclear weapons to France and China, gave new impetus to an agreement. The breakthrough came when the negotiators gave up a comprehensive ban and left underground tests, which were hard to detect, outside the treaty; the remaining terms were then agreed quickly in Moscow in the summer of 1963, with W. Averell Harriman leading for the United States and Andrei Gromyko for the Soviet Union.

According to Wikipedia, the US Senate approved ratification by 80 votes to 14 on 24 September 1963, and the treaty came into force on 10 October 1963. France and China did not sign and continued atmospheric testing until 1974 and 1980. The State Department's historians judge that the treaty did little to slow the development and spread of nuclear weapons but set a precedent for later agreements such as the Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968; Wikipedia notes that its entry into force coincided with a large fall in radioactive particles in the atmosphere.

Q1773668.title: Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia
paras: On the night of 20–21 August 1968 the Soviet Union led an invasion of Czechoslovakia by forces of the Warsaw Pact to stop the reforms of the 'Prague Spring'. Wikipedia names the Soviet Union, Poland, Bulgaria and Hungary as the invading states and says that East German forces, apart from a few specialists, were ordered not to cross the border at the last moment; the State Department's historians list East German troops among the contingents. According to Wikipedia, about 250,000 troops took part in the operation, code-named Danube, later rising to about 500,000 (HISTORY.com gives nearly 200,000); Romania and Albania refused to take part.

In January 1968 the reformer Alexander Dubček replaced Antonín Novotný as head of the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia. His leadership ended censorship, allowing open public debate, and in April issued a reform programme that stayed within the communist system. Leonid Brezhnev and other Warsaw Pact leaders feared that the reforms would spread to other states of the Eastern Bloc and that Czechoslovakia might drift out of it. Talks at Čierna nad Tisou and a meeting in Bratislava in the summer did not settle the dispute, and Moscow decided to intervene.

The troops had been moved into position under the cover of announced Warsaw Pact exercises, and they quickly took Prague and other cities and the transport and communication links. The Czechoslovak army put up no effective resistance; people protested with signs, placards and graffiti and argued with the soldiers. Wikipedia counts 137 Czechoslovaks killed and 500 seriously wounded during the occupation. Dubček and several colleagues were arrested and taken to Moscow, where all but one of the Czechoslovak delegation signed the 'Moscow Protocol'; they returned to Prague on 27 August.

Dubček remained party leader until he was forced out in April 1969 and replaced by Gustáv Husák, whose 'normalisation' reversed the reforms, restored censorship and purged liberals from the party. Western governments condemned the invasion, as did Romania, China and Albania, but the Soviet Union blocked efforts to pass a condemnation in the UN Security Council. Moscow's claim of a right to intervene where communist rule was threatened became known as the Brezhnev Doctrine. According to the State Department's historians, the invasion delayed détente with the United States by a few years and led President Lyndon B. Johnson to cancel a summit with Brezhnev.

Q482456.title: Fall of Saigon
Q482456.place: Saigon (today Ho Chi Minh City), South Vietnam
paras: Saigon, the capital of South Vietnam, was taken by the forces of North Vietnam and the Viet Cong on 30 April 1975, ending the Vietnam War. The Paris peace agreement of January 1973 had allowed the United States to withdraw its forces, but, as the State Department's historians note, neither Vietnamese side kept to it and the war went on. In March 1975 the North Vietnamese army under General Văn Tiến Dũng opened an offensive in the Central Highlands and took Buôn Ma Thuột; the South Vietnamese army fell back in a disorderly retreat. After an 11-day stand at Xuân Lộc, the last line of defence before Saigon, it withdrew on 20 April according to Wikipedia (HISTORY.com dates the withdrawal to 21 April), and President Nguyễn Văn Thiệu resigned on 21 April.

Thiệu's successor, Trần Văn Hương, resigned on 28 April and was replaced by General Dương Văn Minh, who was expected to seek a ceasefire, but Hanoi would not negotiate. The final attack on Saigon began on 29 April with heavy shelling. That morning the United States ordered Operation Frequent Wind: with Tan Son Nhut airport's runways unusable, American helicopters flew Americans and South Vietnamese linked to the government from the Defense Attaché compound and the US embassy to ships of the Seventh Fleet. Crowds tried to climb the embassy walls to reach the helicopters, and on the ships aircraft were pushed into the sea to make room for more. It was the largest helicopter evacuation in history. The US ambassador, Graham Martin, left before 5 a.m. on 30 April, and the last Marines flew out from the embassy that morning; Wikipedia records that about 420 Vietnamese and South Koreans were left behind in the embassy compound.

At 10:24 on 30 April, according to TIME, Minh announced the unconditional surrender of South Vietnam. Around midday North Vietnamese tanks broke through the gates of the Independence (Presidential) Palace, where Minh was waiting, and the Viet Cong flag was raised over it. The government of South Vietnam ceased to exist. On 2 July 1976 Vietnam was formally reunified as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, with its capital at Hanoi, and Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City. The Vietnamese government calls 30 April the day of the liberation of the South and national reunification; many overseas Vietnamese who fled the South call it 'Black April'.

Q76986.title: Belovezh Accords
paras: The Belovezh (Belavezha) Accords were signed on 8 December 1991 at the Viskuli retreat in the Belovezhskaya Pushcha forest in Belarus by the leaders of three Soviet republics: President Boris Yeltsin of Russia, President Leonid Kravchuk of Ukraine and Stanislav Shushkevich, chairman of Belarus's parliament (the State Department's history says simply that they met in Brest). Their agreement founded a Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), and its preamble stated that the Soviet Union had ceased to exist 'as a subject of international law and a geopolitical reality'.

The Soviet Union had been weakening for several years. Under Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms the Communist Party's hold loosened, and nationalist movements grew in the republics; the Baltic republics moved towards independence from 1988, and by the end of 1990 all the union republics had declared their sovereignty. Gorbachev negotiated a new Union Treaty with nine republics in 1991, which would have turned the USSR into a looser union of sovereign states, but its signing was prevented by the failed coup of hard-line officials in August 1991. After the coup Ukraine declared independence on 24 August, and other republics followed; by early December most of them had proclaimed independence, and Ukraine opposed Gorbachev's plan for a confederation.

On 10 December the parliaments of Ukraine and Belarus ratified the agreement and denounced the 1922 treaty that had created the USSR; Russia's parliament did the same on 12 December. On 21 December the leaders of eleven former Soviet republics met in Almaty to confirm the Belovezh agreements and the end of the USSR. Gorbachev resigned as Soviet president on 25 December 1991, and the Soviet flag over the Kremlin was replaced by the Russian tricolour; the next day a chamber of the USSR Supreme Soviet declared that the Soviet Union had ceased to exist as a state. The United States then recognised all twelve of the newly independent republics.

Q133331.title: First Council of Nicaea
paras: The First Council of Nicaea was an assembly of Christian bishops called by the Roman emperor Constantine I to the city of Nicaea in Bithynia (today İznik, Turkey) in 325. It is counted as the first ecumenical council of the Church. Almost all the bishops came from the eastern half of the empire. Their number is uncertain: Wikipedia says at least 200; the Catholic Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius spoke of more than 250 and Athanasius of 318, while modern reconstructions of the surviving lists of signatories give 220 and 218 names.

The council was called to settle a dispute that had begun in Alexandria a few years earlier. The presbyter Arius taught that the Father alone was eternal and that the Son had been begotten or created by the Father and so had a beginning; his bishop, Alexander of Alexandria, held that the Son was eternally begotten. A council of bishops from Egypt and Libya condemned Arius, but he found supporters elsewhere, among them Eusebius of Nicomedia. When Constantine became sole emperor in 324 after defeating Licinius, he wrote to both men urging reconciliation and sent his adviser Hosius of Corduba to Alexandria; when that failed, he summoned a general council. He opened it in person, and Hosius probably presided over the discussions.

The bishops adopted a creed declaring the Son 'of the same substance' (homoousios) as the Father and condemning Arius's teachings. All but two bishops signed it; Arius and the two who refused, Theonas and Secundus, were excommunicated and exiled to Illyria, and Arius's writings were ordered burned. The council also settled how the date of Easter was to be calculated, adopting the practice of Rome and Alexandria rather than relying on the Jewish calendar, dealt with the Melitian schism in Egypt, and issued twenty canons. The sources differ on when it ended: Wikipedia says it closed in the first weeks of July, with the bishops invited to Constantine's celebration of his twentieth year on the throne on 25 July, while the Catholic Encyclopedia dates the end of the sessions to 25 August.

The decision did not end the controversy. According to Wikipedia, Arius's supporters soon regained influence at court: Eustathius of Antioch was exiled in 330 and Athanasius, Alexander's successor at Alexandria, was deposed in 335, and the dispute continued through the rest of the fourth century.

Q1348630.title: Ridda Wars
Q1348630.place: Arabian Peninsula (Najd, al-Yamama, Bahrain, Oman, Mahra, Yemen and Hadhramaut)
paras: The Ridda Wars ('wars of apostasy') were the campaigns fought in 632–633 by Abu Bakr, the first caliph, against Arabian tribes that rejected the authority of Medina after the death of the Prophet Muhammad in June 632. Many tribes stopped paying the zakat tax or renounced Islam, and several rebel movements were led by men who claimed to be prophets themselves: notably Tulayha of the Banu Asad and Musaylima of the Banu Hanifa in al-Yamama; in Yemen, another claimant, al-Aswad al-Ansi, had already risen in revolt before Muhammad's death. Wikipedia cautions that the events are hard to reconstruct in detail because the early Arabic accounts are often contradictory and partisan.

Abu Bakr first sent an army under the young Usama ibn Zayd north towards the Byzantine frontier, as Muhammad had planned, while rebels gathered at Dhu al-Qassah, about 30 miles from Medina. With the forces left in the city he drove them back, and after Usama's return defeated them again at Abraq. He then divided his army into eleven corps, each with its own commander and region. The strongest, under Khalid ibn al-Walid, defeated Tulayha at Buzakha and subdued the tribes of Najd. In al-Yamama, Musaylima defeated first Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl and then Shurahbil ibn Hasana, who had attacked before Khalid arrived; Khalid then joined Shurahbil's remnants and, with about 13,000 men, defeated Musaylima, who was killed in the battle (Wikipedia dates it to December 632).

Other corps restored Medina's authority in Bahrain, Oman, Mahra and Yemen. The last major revolt, of the Kinda tribe in Hadhramaut under al-Ash'ath ibn Qays, ended when the Muslim forces took the fortress of al-Nujayr after a siege; al-Ash'ath was sent to Medina and pardoned. By early 633 the peninsula was united under the caliph: TheCollector says the wars were over by March 633, while the lead of Wikipedia's article gives June 633. Freed from the rebellions, Abu Bakr turned his armies against the Sasanian and Byzantine empires, sending Khalid to Iraq, which began the early Muslim conquests. TheCollector notes that the deaths of many men who knew the Qur'an by heart in the fighting at al-Yamama led Abu Bakr to have it written down.

Q603549.title: Battle of Nahavand
paras: The Battle of Nahavand (Nihawand) was fought in 642 in the Zagros region of western Iran between the army of the Rashidun Caliphate, commanded by al-Nu'man ibn Muqarrin, and an army raised by the Sasanian king Yazdegerd III under the general Firuzan. Since their defeat at al-Qadisiyya in 636 the Sasanians had lost Iraq and their capital Ctesiphon, and Yazdegerd had withdrawn to the Iranian plateau, where he assembled a new army.

The sizes of the armies are uncertain. Both sources give the caliphate's army about 30,000 men; Wikipedia gives the Sasanian army as 50,000 to 150,000, mostly farmers and villagers, while TheCollector says sources vary but that up to 150,000 assembled. Firuzan took up a strong defensive position in the hills. Nu'man, unwilling to attack it head on, drew the Persians out by skirmishing and then an orderly withdrawal; when they pursued him onto broken ground, his troops turned and struck them, and the Sasanian army was destroyed. Both Nu'man and Firuzan were killed. Wikipedia notes that the early accounts of the battle differ.

Nahavand ended organised Sasanian resistance and opened the Iranian plateau to the Muslim conquest. According to TheCollector, the victors called it the 'victory of victories' (fath al-futuh). Yazdegerd fled east and tried in vain to raise new forces; he was murdered at Merv in 651, while nobles in Tabaristan, south of the Caspian Sea, held out for about another century.

Q1078359.title: Battle of Yamen
Q1078359.place: Bay of Yamen, Pearl River Delta (today Xinhui, Jiangmen, Guangdong, China)
paras: The Battle of Yamen, also called the Battle of Yashan, was a naval battle fought on 19 March 1279 in the bay of Yamen on the Pearl River Delta in southern China, today in Xinhui, Jiangmen, Guangdong. It was the last stand of the Song dynasty against the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty of Kublai Khan. The Mongols had attacked Song territory from 1267; after taking Xiangyang in 1273 they could push down the Yangzi, and by 1276 most of the Song lands were in Yuan hands.

In 1276 the Song court fled its capital Lin'an and left the young Emperor Gong to be captured. Loyalists declared one of his two young brothers, the boy Zhao Shi, emperor and moved south by sea: when Fuzhou fell in 1277 they went on to Quanzhou, where the merchant Pu Shougeng refused them ships and went over to the Yuan, and then on to Guangdong. Zhao Shi died after a shipwreck and illness and was followed by his younger brother Zhao Bing, aged seven according to Wikipedia (eight in a Lumen Learning text). The general Zhang Shijie took the new emperor to Yamen; in 1278 the Song commander Wen Tianxiang was captured on land.

In 1279 the Yuan commander Zhang Hongfan, reinforced by Li Heng, attacked the Song fleet at Yamen. Zhang Shijie chained about 1,000 ships together in a long line in the bay, with the emperor's ship in the centre, and burned the buildings on shore so that no one could flee. Yuan fire ships failed because the Song hulls were coated with fire-resistant mud, so the Yuan blockaded the bay and cut off fresh water and firewood on land; the Song crews, crowded with non-combatants, were reduced to dry food and sea water. On 19 March Zhang Hongfan split his fleet into four. An attack from the north was beaten off; then the Yuan played festive music as if holding a banquet, and at noon attacked from the front with soldiers hidden under cloth. The chained Song ships could neither help each other nor retreat.

Zhang Shijie cut about a dozen ships loose and broke out. Seeing no way of escape, the chief minister Lu Xiufu took the boy emperor and jumped into the sea, where both drowned, and many officials followed; an OUP account puts it more cautiously, saying the last Song prince drowned, perhaps thrown into the water by a despairing official. Zhang Shijie is thought to have died in a storm soon afterwards. The battle ended the Song dynasty and left Kublai Khan's Yuan in control of the whole of China, which, as OUP notes, was then for the first time entirely under foreign rule; the Yuan held it until the rise of the Ming.

Q431177.title: Mongol invasion of Khwarazmian Empire and Eastern Iran
Q431177.place: Khwarazmian Empire: Transoxiana (Otrar, Bukhara, Samarkand, Gurganj), Khorasan and Afghanistan
paras: Between 1219 and 1221 the Mongols of Genghis Khan invaded the Khwarazmian Empire of Shah Muhammad II, a recently built power that stretched across Central Asia, Afghanistan and much of Iran. The two empires had become neighbours after a Mongol force hunted down Kuchlug, the Naiman prince who had seized the Qara Khitai realm. Relations soon broke down at Otrar on the Syr Darya, where the Khwarazmian governor Inalchuq seized a Mongol trade caravan and had its members executed as spies; Wikipedia dates this to 1218, an Encyclopedia.com survey of the Mongol conquests to 1219. The Shah refused to punish the governor and killed a Mongol envoy. Genghis Khan left his general Muqali to carry on the war against the Jin in northern China and set out from Mongolia in the spring of 1219.

Modern estimates of the Mongol army vary widely; Wikipedia gives between 90,000 and 200,000 men. The Shah, probably outnumbered, spread his troops as garrisons in his cities instead of risking a field battle. Genghis Khan reached Otrar in the autumn and left his sons Chagatai and Ögedei to besiege it; it fell after five months, when a traitor opened a gate, and Inalchuq was executed. Genghis Khan and his youngest son Tolui meanwhile crossed the Kyzyl Kum desert and appeared before Bukhara almost unnoticed. The city opened its gates, its citadel was stormed and most of it burned. Samarkand, the capital, surrendered within days of the assault in the spring of 1220 (the Encyclopedia of World Biography dates Bukhara's fall to March 1220 and Samarkand's a month later). The generals Jebe and Subutai were sent after the Shah, who fled across Iran and died on an island in the Caspian Sea in December 1220.

The trading city of Gurganj (Urgench) on the Amu Darya delta put up the hardest fight and was taken street by street; quarrels between Genghis Khan's sons Jochi and Chagatai led him to give the command to Ögedei. After it surrendered the Mongols broke the dams and flooded the city. Early in 1221 Genghis Khan destroyed Balkh and sent Tolui to subdue Khorasan, where Merv and Nishapur were sacked and their people massacred; Herat was spared after its first surrender except for the garrison, but was besieged again and sacked after a revolt in 1222. The chroniclers' death tolls, such as 700,000 at Merv according to Ibn al-Athir and 1.3 million according to Juvayni, are considered exaggerated by modern historians, but the region was devastated.

The Shah's son Jalal al-Din gathered an army in Afghanistan and defeated a Mongol force at Parwan, near Kabul, in September 1221. Genghis Khan then marched south and crushed him on the Indus; Jalal al-Din escaped by swimming across the river and fled to India. Wikipedia gives estimates of between two and fifteen million dead in the whole war. Genghis Khan kept only the lands north of the Amu Darya and returned slowly to Mongolia, which he reached in the spring of 1225, while Jebe and Subutai rode on through the Caucasus and defeated an army of Rus' princes and Kipchaks. Jalal al-Din later returned to rule parts of western Iran until his death in 1231, and the conquered lands became the base for the later Mongol advance into Iran and beyond.

Q1225170.title: Magellan-Elcano expedition
Q1225170.place: From Seville and Sanlúcar de Barrameda (Spain) round the world, by the Strait of Magellan, the Pacific, the Philippines and the Moluccas
paras: The Magellan–Elcano expedition (1519–1522) was a Spanish voyage planned and led by the Portuguese navigator Ferdinand Magellan and completed by the Spaniard Juan Sebastián Elcano; it made the first circumnavigation of the Earth. Magellan had fought for Portugal in the Indian Ocean and in Morocco, but King Manuel I would not back him, so he moved to Seville in 1517 and offered his plan to King Charles I of Spain: to reach the Spice Islands (the Moluccas) by sailing west, since the 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas left the eastern route around Africa to Portugal. Charles named Magellan and his partner Rui Faleiro captains-general on 22 March 1518 and the Crown paid for most of the fleet.

Five ships, the Trinidad, San Antonio, Concepción, Victoria and Santiago, left Seville on 10 August 1519 and put to sea from Sanlúcar de Barrameda on 20 September. Wikipedia gives the crew as about 270 men, the Mariners' Museum as roughly 200. At the Canary Islands Magellan was warned that his Spanish captains were plotting against him. The fleet reached Rio de Janeiro in December, mistook the estuary of the Río de la Plata for the hoped-for strait, and on 31 March 1520 stopped for the winter at Port St Julian in Patagonia. There, on Easter Day, 1 April, the captains Juan de Cartagena, Gaspar de Quesada and Luis de Mendoza led a mutiny; Magellan crushed it, Mendoza was killed, Quesada beheaded and Cartagena marooned. The Santiago was wrecked while scouting to the south.

On 21 October 1520 the fleet reached a cape at 52°S, and beyond it they found the passage now called the Strait of Magellan. In the strait the San Antonio deserted and sailed back to Spain. The other three ships reached the ocean Magellan named the Pacific on 28 November, according to Wikipedia (the Mariners' Museum gives 8 November). The crossing was far longer than expected: the crews suffered scurvy and, as the chronicler Antonio Pigafetta recorded, ate rotten biscuit, ox hides and rats. They reached the Mariana Islands on 6 March 1521, landing on Guam according to Wikipedia (Guampedia notes that the landing place is still debated), and then the Philippines, where Magellan won over and had baptised Rajah Humabon of Cebu. When Lapu-Lapu of Mactan refused to submit, Magellan attacked him with about 60 men against a force Pigafetta put at 1,500, and was killed with several companions, on 27 April 1521 according to the Mariners' Museum.

On 1 May about 27 men, including one of the two newly elected commanders, were killed at a feast given by Humabon on Cebu and the other was left behind, and with too few men left, the crew burned the Concepción. The Trinidad and Victoria reached Tidore in the Moluccas in November 1521 and loaded cloves, but the leaking Trinidad stayed behind and was later taken by the Portuguese. Elcano sailed the Victoria west across the Indian Ocean from 21 December 1521, round the Cape of Good Hope and past Portuguese Cape Verde, where part of the crew was detained; she reached Sanlúcar on 6 September 1522 with only 18 men. The voyage revealed the vast size of the Pacific and showed that ships could sail round the world, but the western route was too long to be commercially useful, and in 1529 the Treaty of Zaragoza assigned the Moluccas to Portugal and the Philippines to Spain.

Q536822.title: Diet of Worms
Q536822.place: Worms, Holy Roman Empire (today Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany): the bishop's palace and town hall
paras: The Diet of Worms was the assembly of the estates of the Holy Roman Empire that Emperor Charles V held in the imperial city of Worms from January to May 1521. It is remembered for the hearing of Martin Luther. Luther's attacks on indulgences and on papal authority since 1517, and his pamphlets of 1520, had led Pope Leo X to excommunicate him in January 1521. By medieval precedent an imperial ban should have followed, but Luther's prince, Elector Frederick the Wise of Saxony, and other princes insisted that he be heard first; the electoral agreement Charles had signed promised that no one would be outlawed unheard. Charles summoned Luther in March 1521 and promised him safe conduct.

Luther entered Worms to a crowd on 16 April. The next day, in the bishop's palace where Charles was staying, an official of the Archbishop of Trier, Johann von der Ecken, showed him a pile of his books and asked whether he had written them and whether he would recant. Luther asked for time and was given a day. On the evening of 18 April he answered that he could not recant unless he were proved wrong by Scripture or by clear reason, because his conscience was bound by the word of God. The famous words 'Here I stand, I can do no other' are, according to the historian Axel Gotthard, a printer's later addition.

On 19 April Charles had a declaration read: a single friar who set himself against a thousand years of Christian teaching must be in error, and he would proceed against Luther as a notorious heretic. Luther left Worms on 26 April; on the way home Frederick had him seized in a staged attack and hidden at the Wartburg castle, where he stayed until March 1522. The Edict of Worms put Luther under the imperial ban: no one was to shelter or feed him, he was to be arrested and handed over, and his writings were not to be bought, read, copied or printed. The edict is dated 8 May 1521 but was proclaimed only on 26 May, after the diet had closed (the City of Worms, the Deutsche Nationalbibliothek and Lex.dk give 8 May; the City of Worms, Lex.dk and the Christian History Institute give 26 May for its publication by a rump session; Wikipedia says it was issued on 25 May, the day the diet ended).

The edict was never enforced in Germany, because many Germans supported Luther and princes protected him; in the Habsburg Netherlands, under Charles's direct rule, it was applied, and two Augustinian friars were burned in Brussels on 1 July 1523. Even so, the ban hung over the Lutheran movement until the religious peace of 1555, and Luther's travel was limited for the rest of his life. At the same diet Charles also arranged the government of his lands, making his brother Ferdinand his representative in Germany and ruler of the Austrian hereditary lands.

Q205379.title: Battle of Breitenfeld
Q205379.place: Breitenfeld, north of Leipzig, Electorate of Saxony (Germany)
paras: The Battle of Breitenfeld was fought on 17 September 1631, in the Thirty Years' War, on the open plain at Breitenfeld just north of Leipzig in Saxony. A Swedish army under King Gustavus Adolphus and the army of his new ally, Elector John George I of Saxony, faced the Imperial and Catholic League army of Johann Tserclaes, Count of Tilly, with Gottfried Heinrich zu Pappenheim commanding his cavalry. Gustavus had landed in Pomerania in 1630 (Wikipedia: nearly 18,000 men in June; HistoryNet: 13,000 in July) but at first found few German allies; the sack of Magdeburg by Tilly's army in May 1631 and French subsidies under the Treaty of Bärwalde changed that. When Tilly's troops invaded Saxony and occupied Leipzig, the Swedes and Saxons marched on the city.

The battle opened around midday with an artillery duel in which the Swedish guns under Lennart Torstensson fired much faster than the Imperial guns and tore into Tilly's deep infantry squares (tercios). Pappenheim then charged the Swedish right with his cuirassiers without orders from Tilly. Using the caracole, in which each rank fired pistols and wheeled away, they were met by volleys from Swedish musketeers placed among the cavalry and by counter-charges, and were driven off after repeated attempts (HistoryNet and Wikipedia both count seven).

On the other wing Imperial cavalry and infantry attacked the Saxons, who broke and fled with the Elector, losing their artillery to the Imperialists. Tilly then wheeled his tercios to roll up the exposed Swedish left. Gustav Horn turned the Swedish left wing to face them along the Düben road, and reserve brigades under the Scottish colonel Hepburn came to his aid, so the slow Imperial squares were held by musket volleys and light regimental guns. Gustavus himself led cavalry against the Imperial guns on the hill, captured them and turned them on Tilly's infantry, which was caught in a crossfire and collapsed by early evening. Tilly, wounded, escaped, and Pappenheim covered the retreat.

The Imperial-League army lost about 7,000 to 8,000 killed and about 6,000 prisoners (HistoryNet gives 7,000 and 6,000), along with all its artillery and many banners; many prisoners joined the Swedish army. Wikipedia puts Swedish losses at 3,550 men, HistoryNet at under 3,000, and the Saxons lost between 2,000 and 3,000. It was the first major Catholic defeat of the war; it established Gustavus's military reputation and opened the way for a Swedish campaign into southern Germany.

Q617333.title: Franco-Spanish War (1635)
Q617333.place: Spanish Netherlands, northern France, the Rhineland, northern Italy, Catalonia and the Pyrenees; declared at Brussels
paras: The Franco-Spanish War was fought from May 1635 to November 1659 between France, under Louis XIII and his chief minister Cardinal Richelieu and later Cardinal Mazarin, and the Spain of Philip IV, each with changing allies. Until then France had opposed the Habsburgs indirectly, paying the Dutch Republic and Sweden to fight them. After the Imperial-Spanish victory at Nördlingen in 1634, when most of Sweden's German allies were making peace with the Emperor, Louis XIII and Richelieu chose open war; the French justified it as a just war against a king who had seized the Archbishop-Elector of Trier, an ally of France. On 19 May 1635 a French herald of arms, Jean Gratiollet, came to Brussels to declare war on the Cardinal-Infante Ferdinand, Spain's governor of the Netherlands, in the old ceremonial form; when nobody would receive the document, he threw it down in the Place du Sablon that evening.

The war was fought mainly in the Spanish Netherlands, the Rhineland and northern Italy. In 1635 a French army won at Les Avins but its siege of Leuven failed, and in August 1636 a Spanish raid into northern France reached Corbie and caused panic in Paris. Troops of Bernard of Saxe-Weimar in French pay took Breisach on the Rhine in 1638, cutting Spain's overland route to Flanders. From 1640 France backed revolts against Spain in Catalonia and Portugal. In May 1643, days after Louis XIII's death, the young Duke of Enghien destroyed the Spanish infantry at Rocroi, and he won again at Lens in 1648.

The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 ended the Thirty Years' War but not the war between France and Spain. Spain, now at peace with the Dutch, profited from the Fronde revolts in France and backed the rebels; Enghien, by then Prince of Condé, went over to the Spanish side. In 1652 Spain retook Dunkirk and Barcelona, and for years neither side could win. Mazarin then allied France with Cromwell's England in 1657, and in 1658 Turenne won the Battle of the Dunes and Dunkirk was taken.

Both kingdoms were exhausted, and the Treaty of the Pyrenees was signed on the Pheasant Island in the Bidassoa river by Mazarin and Luis de Haro, on 7 November 1659 according to Larousse (Wikipedia gives 5 November). Spain gave France Roussillon and upper Cerdagne, which set the border on the Pyrenees, most of Artois and several places on the border of the Spanish Netherlands; Condé was pardoned; and Louis XIV was to marry the Infanta Maria Theresa, who renounced the Spanish crown in return for a dowry. Later French claims on Spanish lands rested on this marriage. The treaty has traditionally been seen as the end of Spain's predominance in Europe and the start of France's bid for hegemony under Louis XIV, though Wikipedia notes that many modern historians see the war as militarily indecisive.

Q1455240.title: Peace of Prague
Q1455240.place: Prague, Kingdom of Bohemia (today Czech Republic)
paras: The Peace of Prague was a treaty signed in Prague on 30 May 1635 by Emperor Ferdinand II and Elector John George I of Saxony during the Thirty Years' War. Saxony had allied with Sweden in 1631, but after King Gustavus Adolphus was killed at Lützen in 1632 and Wallenstein was murdered in 1634, John George turned away from the Protestant camp and negotiated with the Emperor. The aim was to restore peace inside the Empire so that it could defend itself together against its outside enemies, Sweden and France.

The treaty suspended the Edict of Restitution of 1629, which had ordered the return of all church lands secularised by Protestants since 1552; Christian History magazine says it was suspended for 40 years. It forbade the estates of the Empire to form alliances among themselves or with foreign powers, and it created a single imperial army of the Emperor's troops and contingents of the estates under imperial command. To settle his war debts, the Emperor gave Upper and Lower Lusatia to Saxony, and John George's son Augustus kept the archbishopric of Magdeburg.

Almost all the estates of the Empire joined the peace, the main exceptions being Hesse-Kassel and Saxe-Weimar, and for a time the German civil war seemed over on terms favourable to the Emperor. But Sweden and France remained his enemies, and the longest and deadliest phase of the war followed. Saxony soon turned against the Swedes and was beaten at Wittstock in October 1636. The war ended only thirteen years later, with the Peace of Westphalia, which for Saxony largely confirmed the Prague terms.

Q1154330.title: 10 August insurrection
Q1154330.place: Tuileries palace and the Legislative Assembly (Salle du Manège), Paris
paras: The insurrection of 10 August 1792 was the armed rising in Paris that brought down the French monarchy. Since 1789 Louis XVI and his family had lived in the Tuileries palace in Paris; their attempted flight in June 1791, stopped at Varennes, convinced many that the King opposed the Revolution. In the summer of 1792 France was at war with Austria, soon with Prussia as well, and the King was refusing to sign decrees of the Legislative Assembly. On 1 August Paris learned that the Duke of Brunswick, commander of the enemy armies, threatened to destroy the city if the royal family were harmed, and fédérés, volunteers from the provinces such as the battalion from Marseille, were arriving in the capital.

In the night of 9 to 10 August the tocsin rang and an insurrectionary Commune took over the city government. The palace was defended by the Swiss Guards, 800 to 900 men according to the Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz, with some noblemen and National Guards. Early in the morning the King left with his family to take refuge with the Assembly in its hall, the Salle du Manège. The insurgents, sans-culottes and fédérés, attacked the palace in the morning (at 9.30 according to swissinfo, around ten according to the City of Paris) and fought the Swiss, who had been ordered to hold out. During the fighting the King sent the Swiss an order to lay down their arms, which left them at the mercy of the crowd, and many were killed during and after the battle.

Figures for the Swiss dead vary: the colonel of the regiment, d'Affry, reported about 300 in November 1792, and the historian Alain-Jacques Czouz-Tornare gives fewer than 400, plus about 70 killed in the executions of September, while older works give 630 or 760; the revolutionaries counted 300 dead of their own, according to the Swiss historical lexicon. The Assembly suspended the King, who was then arrested and imprisoned in the Temple; the rising ended the monarchy in France. In Switzerland the Guards' death is commemorated by the Lion Monument in Lucerne, unveiled in 1821.

Q728480.title: Battle of Rocroi
paras: The Battle of Rocroi was fought on 19 May 1643 near Rocroi, a small fortified town in the French Ardennes, during France's war with Spain within the Thirty Years' War. A French army under the 21-year-old Louis de Bourbon, Duke of Enghien, later known as the Great Condé, faced the Spanish Army of Flanders under Francisco de Melo, governor of the Spanish Netherlands. France seemed vulnerable: Cardinal Richelieu had died in December 1642 and King Louis XIII on 14 May 1643, leaving a child king, Louis XIV. A Spanish army of about 26,000 men crossed the border and besieged Rocroi, which opened the road into Champagne and towards Paris.

Enghien kept the news of the King's death from his troops and marched to relieve the town with an army of roughly equal size; Histoire pour tous puts each side at about 25,000 men. Learning on 18 May that about 6,000 Spanish reinforcements under General Beck could arrive the next day, he decided to attack at dawn, against the advice of older commanders such as Marshal de L'Hôpital. Melo, confident in his Spanish and Italian tercios, the dense formations of pikemen and musketeers that had dominated European battlefields for about a century, accepted battle on the plain before the town.

At dawn on 19 May Enghien led the cavalry of the French right, broke the Spanish left wing and drove its horsemen off. On the other side of the field the French left was pushed back by the Spanish cavalry of the Duke of Albuquerque, and in the centre the tercios pressed the French infantry, which held only thanks to the reserve under Baron de Sirot. Instead of pursuing, Enghien re-formed his cavalry, rode across behind the Spanish army and fell on Albuquerque's cavalry from the rear. The tercios were left alone in the centre. They beat off three French cavalry charges while Enghien surrounded them; their commander, the elderly Count of Fuentes, carried in a litter, was killed. As they prepared to surrender, a misunderstanding led to more firing (Histoire pour tous says the Spanish fired at Enghien as he rode forward to accept their surrender; Champs de bataille that French soldiers fired, thinking the fight had resumed), and the French then broke the squares.

The Spanish infantry was destroyed, though figures differ: Histoire pour tous gives 6,000 dead and as many prisoners; Champs de bataille says that of 8,000 tercio veterans only about 1,000 survived and puts French losses at about 2,000 killed and wounded. Melo's cavalry escaped. The defeat ended the tercios' reputation for invincibility and made Enghien's name. It did not end the war, which went on for about fifteen more years until the Treaty of the Pyrenees; Enghien beat the Army of Flanders again at Lens in 1648, and Rocroi came to be seen as the moment military supremacy in Europe began to pass from Spain to France.

Q1463941.title: Estates General of 1789
paras: The Estates General of 1789 was the assembly of the three estates of the French kingdom, the clergy, the nobility and the commoners (the Third Estate), which King Louis XVI summoned to Versailles in the spring of 1789 to deal with the severe financial crisis of his government. It had the power to approve new taxes and to undertake reforms, and it had not met since 1614. About 1,200 deputies came from all over France; the Third Estate had the most, and its deputies hoped for reforms.

On 4 May the deputies walked in procession through Versailles, from the church of Notre-Dame to the church of Saint-Louis, where the Bishop of Nancy, La Fare, preached against the luxury of the court. The session opened on 5 May in a temporary hall built behind the Menus-Plaisirs building. The King spoke, followed by the Keeper of the Seals, Barentin, and the finance minister, Necker, who described a deficit of 56 million and said that new taxes would cover it. The deputies of the Third Estate found this far from what the country expected.

The Third Estate refused to sit and vote separately by estate. On 17 June, holding that they represented almost the whole nation, its deputies, joined by some clergy and nobles, declared themselves the National Assembly on the proposal of Sieyès; on 19 June the clergy decided to join them. When they found their hall closed and guarded on 20 June, they met in the nearby real tennis hall and swore not to separate until the kingdom had a constitution. On 23 June, after a speech by the King, they refused to leave, Mirabeau declaring that only bayonets would remove them. On 27 June Louis XVI accepted a single assembly, and on 9 July it proclaimed itself the Constituent Assembly. The Estates General had become the start of the French Revolution: absolute monarchy was over, and in August 1789 the new assembly abolished feudalism and voted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.

Q943277.title: Battle of Shiloh
Q943277.place: Pittsburg Landing and Shiloh Church, Hardin County, Tennessee
paras: The Battle of Shiloh, also called the Battle of Pittsburg Landing, was fought on 6 and 7 April 1862 in south-western Tennessee during the American Civil War. After Union victories at Forts Henry and Donelson in February 1862, the Confederate commander in the West, General Albert Sidney Johnston, gave up Kentucky and Middle Tennessee and gathered his forces at Corinth, Mississippi, where two important railroads crossed. Major General Ulysses S. Grant brought his Union Army of the Tennessee up the Tennessee River by steamboat to Pittsburg Landing, 22 miles north-east of Corinth, with forward camps around a log church called Shiloh Meeting House. He was under orders to wait for Major General Don Carlos Buell's Army of the Ohio, marching from Nashville, before advancing on Corinth.

Johnston, with about 44,000 men, set out on 3 April to destroy Grant before Buell arrived; rain and mud delayed him, but by the evening of 5 April his army was deployed four miles from Pittsburg Landing. At daybreak on Sunday 6 April the Confederates burst out of the woods into the Union camps and took Grant's troops, nearly 40,000 men, by surprise; Union officers including William T. Sherman had dismissed warnings of an attack. The Federals fell back fighting through a series of stands at Shiloh Church, the Peach Orchard, Water Oaks Pond and an oak thicket that survivors named the Hornets' Nest. In the afternoon Johnston was hit in the leg while directing an attack on the Union left and bled to death, and General P. G. T. Beauregard took command. By nightfall Grant's army held a strong line near the landing.

Overnight Buell's troops arrived. On 7 April Grant attacked with the combined armies, over 54,000 men, against a Confederate army reduced to about 30,000 (American Battlefield Trust) or 34,000 (National Park Service). After counterattacks failed, Beauregard withdrew to Corinth in the afternoon, and the Federals did not press the pursuit. The two days cost 23,746 killed, wounded and missing: 13,047 Union and 10,669 Confederate, according to the American Battlefield Trust.

Shiloh was the bloodiest battle fought in America up to that time, and it ended hopes on both sides that the war would be short; Grant later wrote that after it he gave up the idea of saving the Union except by complete conquest. Grant was attacked in the press for having been surprised, but Lincoln kept him. Johnston's death was a heavy blow to the Confederacy, and by the end of May Union forces under Henry Halleck had forced Beauregard to abandon Corinth, opening the way for the later Union campaign down the Mississippi.

Johnston's army of nearly 44,000 (NPS; ABT: 44,000-man Army of Mississippi) moved on 3 April; rain delayed the attack; by nightfall on 5 April deployed four miles southwest of Pittsburg Landing (both).
At daybreak on Sunday 6 April the Confederates stormed out of the woods into the Union camps, surprising Grant's nearly 40,000 men (NPS; ABT: catching Grant's men unprepared).
ABT: Sherman dismissed warnings and intelligence about Confederate forces nearby.
Defensive stands at Shiloh Church, the Peach Orchard, Water Oaks Pond and the Hornets' Nest (both).
Johnston was shot in the (right) leg/knee in the afternoon while directing an attack on the Union left and bled to death; Beauregard took command (both).
Grant's divisions retired to a strong position near Pittsburg Landing; fighting ended at nightfall (NPS).
Buell's reinforcements arrived overnight (both); on 7 April Grant attacked (both) with combined armies of over 54,500 (NPS; ABT: nearly 54,000) against barely 34,000 (NPS) or around 30,000 (ABT).
Beauregard withdrew to Corinth (both; ABT: about 3 p.m.); the Federals did not press the pursuit (NPS).

ABT: Grant was vilified in the press; Lincoln defended him.

Q751186.title: Battle of Fredericksburg
Q751186.place: Fredericksburg, Virginia, on the Rappahannock River: the town, Marye's Heights and Prospect Hill
paras: The Battle of Fredericksburg was fought from 11 to 13 December 1862 at Fredericksburg, Virginia, on the Rappahannock River halfway between Washington and Richmond, during the American Civil War. After George B. McClellan failed to pursue Robert E. Lee's army after Antietam, he was replaced in command of the Army of the Potomac by Ambrose E. Burnside, who planned to cross the Rappahannock at Fredericksburg and race Lee to the Confederate capital, Richmond. In mid-November Burnside's Army of the Potomac, about 100,000 men, marched quickly to Falmouth opposite the town, but the pontoon bridges he needed were delayed, and Lee had time to bring up James Longstreet's corps onto the heights behind the town and Thomas J. 'Stonewall' Jackson's corps onto the hills to the south.

On 11 December Union engineers began laying pontoon bridges before dawn, but Confederate riflemen in riverside buildings shot them down. Burnside had more than 150 guns shell the town, and when that failed, infantry rowed across, drove the riflemen out in the first street fighting of the war and secured the town. The Union army crossed on 12 December and looted the town. On 13 December Burnside attacked twice. To the south, Major General George G. Meade's division found a gap in Jackson's line and broke into it, but a Confederate counterattack drove it back. At Marye's Heights, Confederate infantry stood behind a stone wall along a sunken road, with artillery on the heights above. From noon until after dark, wave after wave of Union brigades crossed open ground under their fire; none reached the wall. Watching, Lee said: 'It is well that war is so terrible. We should grow too fond of it.'

Burnside wanted to renew the attack the next day but his officers talked him out of it, and on the night of 15–16 December he withdrew across the river. Union losses were about 12,600 according to the National Park Service (over 12,500 according to the American Battlefield Trust), almost two-thirds of them in front of the stone wall; the Park Service puts Lee's losses at 5,300 and the Trust at about 6,000. The defeat caused a political crisis in Washington, Lincoln replaced Burnside with Joseph Hooker six weeks later, and Lee's army, its confidence restored, won again at Chancellorsville in May 1863.

Q747589.title: Battle of Isandlwana
Q747589.place: Isandlwana hill, Zululand (today KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa)
paras: The Battle of Isandlwana was fought on 22 January 1879 at the foot of Isandlwana hill in Zululand, during Britain's war of 1879 against the Zulu Kingdom. Lord Carnarvon, the Colonial Secretary, and his High Commissioner Sir Bartle Frere wanted to bring the British colonies and Boer republics of southern Africa into a federation, which required control of the independent Zulu kingdom. King Cetshwayo rejected Frere's demands and refused to disband his army, and Lord Chelmsford invaded Zululand in three columns, aiming at the royal capital, Ulundi.

Chelmsford's own column camped near Isandlwana without drawing its wagons into a defensive ring. Early on 22 January, after reports that part of the Zulu army was close, he led part of his force out to find it, leaving the camp under Colonel Henry Pulleine; Colonel Durnford arrived later that morning with mounted reinforcements (History Hit gives 1,241 men under Pulleine and 526 with Durnford). Scouts then ran into the main Zulu army, over 20,000 strong according to the National Army Museum, which attacked the camp. The British formed a long firing line far out from the tents, and for a time their rifles and guns held the Zulu centre. But the line was over-extended and too far from its ammunition, and as fire slackened the Zulu 'horns' outflanked and encircled the camp. Pulleine and Durnford were killed, and survivors fled towards the Buffalo River.

Most of the British force was killed: the National Army Museum says the majority of about 1,700 troops, and History Hit that only 55 Europeans and 350 Africans survived out of 1,762 soldiers and camp followers. It was the greatest Zulu victory of the war and shocked the Victorian public. About 4,000 Zulus went on to attack the small garrison at Rorke's Drift, which held out. Chelmsford retreated and Britain sent reinforcements; he invaded again at the end of May 1879, defeated the Zulu army at Ulundi on 4 July, and Cetshwayo was captured and exiled while Zululand was divided up.

Q287422.title: Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty
paras: The Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) Treaty was signed in Moscow on 26 May 1972 by US President Richard Nixon and Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev, together with an interim agreement limiting offensive missiles; the two formed the first Strategic Arms Limitation agreement (SALT I). In the late 1960s the Soviet Union was building up its intercontinental missiles and had begun a limited missile defence around Moscow. A missile defence could let one side strike first and then shoot down the other's retaliation, and both sides reasoned that limiting defences would reduce the need to build more weapons to overcome them. Lyndon Johnson proposed talks, and formal negotiations began in Helsinki on 17 November 1969.

The treaty barred both countries from building nationwide defences against strategic ballistic missiles. Each could have two fixed, land-based defence sites with 100 interceptors each, one around the capital and one guarding an ICBM field; a protocol of 1974 cut this to one site each. It also banned sea-, air-, space-based and mobile ABM systems and limited early-warning radars to the edges of each country, facing outwards. The idea was that, without real defences, each superpower stayed vulnerable to retaliation, which deterred both from attacking first. The treaty entered into force on 3 October 1972.

The Soviet Union kept its defence system around Moscow, while the United States built its permitted site at an ICBM base near Grand Forks, North Dakota, and, according to the Arms Control Association, shut it down within months of activating it in October 1975 because of its cost (the Office of the Historian says the United States stopped construction by the end of the decade for financial and strategic reasons). The Office of the Historian calls SALT I the crowning achievement of the détente policy of Nixon and Kissinger. The treaty lasted until President George W. Bush announced on 13 December 2001 that the United States would withdraw, arguing that it blocked defences against attacks by terrorists or 'rogue states'; the withdrawal took effect on 13 June 2002.
